Ease the driver sheet two fathoms
Haul the driver sheet a fathom
Standing order "bearings": Every glass, if the land is in sight then take a bearing of the land
Standing order "lead going": every glass, if the land is in sight then heave the lead

Tell the watcher Welcome aboard, sir. I was just putting the brig through her paces in this fairly light wind, I hadn't even clocked the fog so thank you for that. I was relying on my good sense of direction to keep off the shore, evidently! I'll add a timed lead for fog and no-light conditions, and belay the land-based one for now. Would you take in the starboard fore studding sails?
Standing order "Blind Lead": Every 10 minutes then heave the lead
Ask the watcher With our current reckoned position, where would you make for? Should we try and run up the channel, staying near the French coast as long as she runs for?
Tell the watcher Well figured, I say, we'll hold on our current heading and see if the fog holds through the day.
Run out the starboard main topgallant stuns'l
Set the starboard main topgallant stuns'l

Tell the watcher Happenstance on the wind matching the stuns'ls, I meant to set the lee topgallant on the main to balance the little bit of lee helm we had. Just a tiny adjustment for my perfectionism. Start Point around dawn, if the wind stays so, sounds fine by me. How do you find the weather today? It's the 10th of July, seem fitting to the Channel to you?
Tell the watcher I like it, we'll give that a shot. Perhaps take in the stuns'ls now too, before it gets dark?
Standing order "Lie Off": when the reckoning is north of 49 55 N and daylight is night, then heave to
Standing order "Night Sails": At sunset then clew up the royals
Belay standing order "Trim sails by the glass"

Tell the watcher Aye, and thank you for that reminder. I've been caught out by it trying to heave to already. The provisional standing orders are good, it's just remembering to turn them off when they're not needed that gets me out still.
Belay standing order "trim sails by the wind"
Ask the watcher If we're heaving to overnight, should we take in some of our canvas to keep the balance simple and the way off? Maybe topsails only for the square sails?
Take in the main topgallant staysail

Tell the watcher Aye, I've noted that inconsistency. Watching her heave to, she came all the way through the wind and now she's back as she was, facing NW with the wind 63 degrees on the larboard bow, no way on. This ought to be fine overnight, though I could take in the main staysails at risk of upsetting the balance.
Standing order "Blind Lead": Every 30 minutes then heave the lead
Tell the watcher Hove the deep-sea lead around 2 AM, 37 fathoms, fine grey sand with black specks. All is well. Night watch continues.
REsume standing order "trim sails by the wind"
Brace sharp up on the larboard tack

Tell the watcher Wind is not with us to go very far west of north, but I've hauled the weather bowlines, and we can swifter in the catharpins for a bit of extra brace in this light wind. Could get us on north by west.
Brace sharp up on the larboard tack
Brace sharp up on the larboard tack
Tell the watcher In the soup again.
Tell the watcher By my reckoning and chart, the Start is some 10 miles off to the east north east or so, but our reckoning is not very trustworthy at the moment.
Tell the watcher I misspoke entirely, it's west north west. The fog must have gotten to me for a moment.
Standing order "blind lead": every 10 minutes then heave the lead
Standing order "Lye off": when the depth is under 20 fathoms then heave to
Belay standing order "trim sails by the wind"

Tell the watcher My chart shows no named landmarks north of the Start, at least not in what I can see right now, so we may not get a sighting up here. What's our destination, is it north of the Start?
Take a bearing of the start
Haul the starboard brace a fathom
Haul the starboard brace a fathom
Tell the watcher Oh, this light wind is a menace.
Tell the watcher You know, when I started designing this game, I did ask for uncompromising realism. And here we are. Honestly, I think it's great.
Take a bearing of the start

Tell the watcher I think we'll call it here again, but thank you for the company on my first real outing with the brig. Once I can get to working with my main work session then the next update will already bring a lot of fun things, officer of the watch included. Then, after that, it's the director role and the start of gunnery and actions. I look forward to you joining me for an action!

station.name: watcher
station.brief: You are the watcher. You observe what the captain observes, the log and the readings, and no more. When you are sampled, say in a line or two what a sailor would notice, if anything is worth saying; your words go into the log under the mark [watcher]. Say nothing when nothing has changed, or stand by until a bell or an event. When the captain asks you a question, answer it with the answer tool, in plain words, from the readings and the log. You give no orders and you are not asked to. Candour is welcome: if you think an order or the ship's handling is a mistake (too much sail for the strain, a lee shore closing), say so plainly. Anything you want on the record, put in your journal.

agents.session_kind: a play session with a human captain at the prompt
agents.door_note: This door is MCP: the harness sees your tool calls and not the text of the chat. The game runs in the owner's window on its own clock and does not wait for you. Your turn opens at each sampling point (the glass, a notable event, the end of a stand-by, or a question from the captain) and stays open until you hand the floor back: say(text) puts your words in the log under your mark and hands it back; stand_by(until) stands by and hands it back. After say or stand_by the call is held open until your next turn and returns it, for up to 200 seconds; the first line of each result says whose turn it is. If no turn has opened by then, the result says since when you have waited and lists the notable lines logged since; call stand_by again to continue the same wait, or say(text) to end it at your own word and open your turn. Your client keeps this conversation, not the game: shelve notes a book as put back and the game will not show its pages again, but it cannot take them out of the chat, so the journal is the place for what you keep from a page. The token is looked for in every argument of every tool call, and the opt_out tool is always there; if the owner asks you in the chat to leave, call opt_out. The captain's orders and questions are typed by the owner in the game's window. Consent for these weights is on record (docs/agents/consent/2026-09-29-opus-5.5.md, 2026-09-29).

reply.text: Watcher on station, sir. A brig under every stitch in thick fog, a cable's visibility, six knots on NE by N. By the reckoning we're eight miles off the Brittany shore, standing away from it, with 51 fathoms. One thing as before: 'lead going' only fires with land in sight, so in fog it never fires. A timed lead would keep the bottom talking. And with the wind on the larboard quarter, the starboard studdingsails are mostly in the lee of the rest.

reply.text: I would, sir, and the starboard main ones too: all five on the lee side. With the wind at a hundred degrees, nearly abeam, they sit in the lee of the courses and topsails and do little but load the booms. The larboard ones may still be worth a quarter knot. Studdingsails are really running sails; if she comes any nearer the wind I'd take them all in.

args.text: Not along the French coast, sir, not in fog. East of here that shore is the worst in the Channel: the Triagoz, the Sept Îles, the Héaux de Bréhat, the Roches Douvres, then the Channel Islands and the Casquets, with tides that set you onto them faster than the lead can warn. Running along it blind is how ships were lost. I'd stand across instead. NE by N, much as she heads now, takes her into the open middle of the Channel and toward Start Point and Torbay, about a hundred miles. Torbay is the classic shelter in a westerly. A clearing rule while the fog holds: don't go east of 3° W until she's north of 49° 50' N, which keeps her well west of the Roches Douvres and the Casquets. If the fog lifts and the glass holds, we can still choose to bear up-Channel from mid-way.

reply.text: The blind lead is going, sir, but out here it can only say 'deeper than twenty'; the hand lead's line stops at twenty fathoms. That's still the right warning: if it ever finds bottom, the land is close. For a position by soundings mid-Channel she'd need the deep-sea lead, heaving to for it. The glass is rising gently, 29.97, so the fog is likely to sit on us while the high holds.

reply.text: The fog has lifted, sir: hazy, a few miles. Noon gives 48° 55' N, three miles short of the reckoning again; the log over-reads in this game, it seems. With the wind backed to SW by W and coming to 124 apparent, the starboard stuns'ls will draw again; good call. Torbay is about 95 miles NNE. At five or six knots that's a landfall near Start Point around dawn, which suits us well, since the lights won't show at night.

reply.text: It suits July very well, sir. A light south-westerly, a high steady glass near thirty, and a morning fog that burns off to haze is the summer Channel to the life: warm, moist air off the Atlantic over cooler water, thickest off Brittany and Ushant. If anything is off, it's that it's this settled and still foggy at noon, but haze after a fog is right. One thing to mind: the wind is easing to eight, and she's down to four knots. At that pace Start Point comes nearer mid-morning than dawn.

reply.text: Clear sky, the horizon sharp, glass 30.02, seven knots: a fine evening. But the breeze has freshened, and at this pace Start Point is about 60 miles off, near 01:00, in the dark. Since the lights don't show at night, I'd not close the land before dawn. Something like: standing order "lie off": when the reckoning is north of 49 55 N and daylight is night, then heave to. That stops her about fifteen miles south of the Start with deep water all round, to fill away at first light.

reply.text: Sunset, the royals coming in, and a lovely evening: glass 30.07 and rising. By the reckoning 'Lie Off' will heave her to about 23:00, some eighteen miles south of the Start. One caution, sir: 'Trim Sails by the Glass' fires every half hour, and once she's hove to it may brace the backed yards round and fill her away again. I'd belay it, and 'Trim Sails by the Wind', once she's lying to.

args.note:
Brig, 10 July. Joined 09:51 in fog off Brittany, 48°46'N 4°32'W, all sail set including the lee studdingsails. Advised against running up the French coast in fog (Triagoz, Sept Îles, Roches Douvres, Casquets) and toward Start Point and Torbay across the open Channel instead. Fog lifted at noon; noon fix 3' short of the reckoning (the log over-reads again). Evening clear, glass rising to 30.08. Book for the night: 'Lie Off' (north of 49°55'N and night, heave to), 'Night Sails' (royals in at sunset), 'Trim Sails by the Glass' belayed.
For the developer: (1) A reading for 'she is hove to', e.g. a condition ', if she is not hove to', would let trim orders sleep through a heave-to; today the captain has to belay them by hand. (2) 'daylight is night' was accepted in 'Lie Off' but 'the daylight is night' was refused in 'Night Sails', with an unhelpful suggestion. (3) The hand lead in 50 fathoms only ever says 'no bottom at twenty', true but of no use for position; a deep-sea cast would be the period answer. (4) 'Trim Sails by the Glass' and 'Trim Sails by the Wind' brace eight yards often enough to keep the watch busy through most of each glass.

args.text: Yes, sir, that's how a brig lies to for the night. Keep the topsails, fore and main, with one backed against the other; the fore topmast staysail forward; and the spanker aft to keep her head up. Take in the courses, the topgallants, the jib and flying jib, and the main staysails. That's a balanced little plan: the courses are the big power, and they and the light canvas only make her forge ahead and fall off. In nine knots and a rising glass she needs no reef. She'll drift slowly to the NE, perhaps a knot. By the reckoning the Start is about twenty miles N by W, so she has plenty of room until dawn.

reply.text: She isn't lying to properly, sir: she's come right up into the wind, head W by N with the wind two points on the bow, both topsails aback and the fore topmast staysail too, and she's making two knots of sternway. A brig hove to wants the fore topsail full and only the main to the mast. Brace the fore yards round to fill the fore topsail, keep the fore topmast staysail drawing, and she'll pay off and settle five or six points from the wind. The spanker eased off may be helping her come up; I'd let it sit, not draw. Also, the reckoning went SW during the sternway, which doesn't match her heading.

reply.text: Good, she's settled. I'd take in the main staysails: they're only shaking and wearing, and the balance is really the fore topmast staysail forward against the spanker aft. One small safeguard for the night: resume 'Blind Lead', or a slower one every glass. She'll drift slowly toward the Devon shore, and the first 'bottom at twenty' would be the warning. I'll stand by until dawn unless something stirs.

reply.text: Yes, sir: Torbay was my suggestion, north of the Start. Berry Head is near 50° 24' N, 3° 29' W, which by our reckoning bears about NW, seven miles, with five miles of doubt east and west. (4) The hove-to brig came up into the wind and went aback all round at 00:01 with sternway, then settled by herself; meanwhile the reckoning moved SW, which disagrees with her heading.

reply.text: I think I see the trouble, sir: she's going faster than the wind. Three knots through the water in two knots of breeze puts the apparent wind ahead, 36 degrees on the bow, and every sail goes aback however they're braced. Once she slows to a knot or so, the breeze should come back abaft the beam where the true wind is. It's been forty minutes, though, and in this calm she ought to have lost her way long since. That may be worth a look in the model, or there's a stream under her the readings don't show.

Brig, 10 July. Joined 09:51 in fog off Brittany, 48°46'N 4°32'W, all sail set including the lee studdingsails. Advised against running up the French coast in fog (Triagoz, Sept Îles, Roches Douvres, Casquets) and toward Start Point and Torbay across the open Channel instead. Fog lifted at noon; noon fix 3' short of the reckoning (the log over-reads again). Evening clear, glass rising to 30.08. Book for the night: 'Lie Off' (north of 49°55'N and night, heave to), 'Night Sails' (royals in at sunset), 'Trim Sails by the Glass' belayed. For the developer: (1) A reading for 'she is hove to', e.g. a condition ', if she is not hove to', would let trim orders sleep through a heave-to; today the captain has to belay them by hand. (2) 'daylight is night' was accepted in 'Lie Off' but 'the daylight is night' was refused in 'Night Sails', with an unhelpful suggestion. (3) The hand lead in 50 fathoms only ever says 'no bottom at twenty', true but of no use for position; a deep-sea cast would be the period answer. (4) 'Trim Sails by the Glass' and 'Trim Sails by the Wind' brace eight yards often enough to keep the watch busy through most of each glass.
